title: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
summary: How Chromium, Firefox and WebKit split the browser into sandboxed processes, why Spectre forced site isolation, where IPC and JIT bugs break through, and how fixes race n-days.
outcomes: Map Chromium's browser, renderer, GPU, network and utility processes and compare them with Firefox Fission and WebKit
Explain site isolation's process locks, jail and citadel checks, and why Spectre made them necessary
Review an IPC or Mojo handler for trusted-origin and handle bugs and write the browser-side fix
Explain JIT type confusion and bounds-check elimination bugs and the V8 sandbox, pointer cage and JIT policy
Apply the Rule of 2 and explain MiraclePtr, Rust components and RLBox as memory-safety strategy
Read in-the-wild cases (CVE-2023-4863, CVE-2021-30551, CVE-2025-2783) for bug class, boundary and fix

lessons.title: A browser runs hostile code all day: the threat model

blocks.md:
Plain idea: every web page you open is a program written by a stranger, and your browser runs it. Most programs are attacked only when someone finds a way in; a browser is handed attacker-written HTML, images, fonts and JavaScript on every click. So browser vendors start from an unusual assumption: some of that content **will** find a memory bug, and the design must decide what the attacker gets when it does.

Tiny example: you open a news page with an advert in a frame. If the advert's script finds a bug in the code that parses a WebP image, that script now runs machine code of its choosing inside the browser. The rest of this course is about where that code is running, what it can reach next, and how vendors and defenders shrink both.

Recall two things from the prerequisites. From **The browser security model**: the same-origin policy is enforced by checks inside the browser's own code, and site isolation puts different sites in different operating-system processes as a second wall. From **OS security, privilege and isolation**: Chromium's sandbox uses a **broker** (the privileged browser process) and **targets** (sandboxed processes), and its design document says to treat sandboxed code as malicious once it is past a few early calls in `main()`.

This course opens those walls up. A **renderer** is the process that turns a page into pixels (it *renders* it): it parses HTML and CSS, decodes images and runs JavaScript. A **compromised renderer** is one where attacker code already runs. The browser's whole design asks: what can a compromised renderer still not do?

The numbers explain the assumption. The Chromium project reports that about 70% of its high-severity security bugs are memory-safety problems, counted over [912 high or critical bugs affecting Stable since 2015](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/memory-safety/), and that half of those are use-after-free bugs. Samuel Gross of the V8 team (V8 is Chrome's JavaScript engine) wrote in [the V8 sandbox announcement](https://v8.dev/blog/sandbox) that every Chrome exploit caught in the wild from 2021 to 2023 started with memory corruption in a renderer, and 60% of those bugs were in V8.

Two words for the rest of the course. A **0-day** is a bug attackers use before the vendor has shipped a fix. An **n-day** is, in the Chrome team's words, the [exploitation of a known and patched security issue](https://security.googleblog.com/2023/08/an-update-on-chrome-security-updates.html) against people who have not yet installed the fix.

blocks.title: The attacker's ladder inside a browser

scenes.caption: The pieces: an attacker's page, the sandboxed renderer that runs it, the privileged processes it talks to, and the operating system underneath.
Step one is free: any page runs its script in a renderer. Nothing has gone wrong yet; this is the web working as designed.
A memory bug in the renderer (a JIT bug, an image decoder overflow) gives code execution inside the sandbox. Chromium rates this High.
The renderer can only ask other processes for things over IPC (inter-process communication). A bug in how the browser, GPU or network process handles those requests is a sandbox escape.
Outside the sandbox the attacker has the user's privileges. A kernel bug can go further still. Each rung is a separate bug, and a separate chance to stop or detect them.

blocks.md:
Chromium writes this ladder into its [security severity guidelines](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/severity-guidelines.md), which decide how fast a bug must be fixed:

- **Critical**: lets an attacker read or write arbitrary resources with the user's privileges, for example memory corruption in the browser process reachable from web content *without* first compromising the renderer, or a full chain from web content to code outside the sandbox. Target: patch deployed to all users in under 30 days.
- **High**: code execution inside the sandbox (a renderer bug); a sandbox escape that needs a compromised renderer first; or a site isolation bypass, such as two sites unexpectedly sharing a renderer. Target: under 60 days.
- **Medium** and **Low**: limited reads or writes, or bugs with strong mitigating factors.

If there is evidence of exploitation in the wild, the bug is treated as top priority whatever its rating, with a target of 7 days or less.

blocks.caption: A toy triage helper that encodes the guideline's main cases. Real triage weighs many more factors.

blocks.code:
JIT type confusion                High: code runs inside the sandbox
Broker trusts a renderer handle   High: sandbox escape, needs a renderer bug first
Browser overflow from page data   Critical: privileged process reached from a web page
Two sites share one renderer      High: one site reads another site's data

blocks.md: Misconception: "a sandbox escape is worse than a renderer bug, so it must be Critical." Chromium rates a renderer sandbox escape **High** because it needs the precondition of a compromised renderer. Critical is reserved for bugs that reach privileged code straight from a web page, or full chains.

**What this course covers, and what it leaves out.** You will see how Chromium, Firefox and WebKit split the browser into processes; how site isolation and the IPC boundary hold against a compromised renderer; why JavaScript engines are the favourite target and how vendors contain them; the memory-safety strategy behind new code; real in-the-wild cases at the level of vendor advisories and root-cause analyses; and the patch gap that turns every public fix into an n-day race. How attackers turn a bug into a working exploit is deliberately out of scope; the course **Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel** discusses exploit chains conceptually.

blocks.question: A memory-corruption bug lets a malicious page run code inside Chrome's sandboxed renderer, but nothing more. How does Chromium's severity guideline rate it?
options: Low, because the sandbox contains it
Critical, because any code execution is Critical
High: code execution within the confines of the sandbox
Medium, because it needs JavaScript
blocks.explain: The guideline's High examples include memory corruption in the renderer: arbitrary code inside the sandbox. Critical needs privileged code reached from web content or a full chain out of the sandbox. Low is for bugs with extreme mitigating factors.

blocks.question: Why do browser vendors design as if the renderer is already compromised?
options: Because renderers parse attacker-controlled content in large C++ code bases, and memory bugs there keep being found and exploited
Because renderers run with administrator rights
Because the same-origin policy is not enforced in renderers
Because JavaScript cannot be sandboxed
blocks.explain: Renderers handle hostile input all day, and Chromium's own data shows memory-safety bugs dominate high-severity issues, with all 2021 to 2023 in-the-wild Chrome exploits starting in a renderer. Renderers run with fewer rights, not more.

lessons.title: Chromium's processes: browser, renderer, GPU, network, utility

blocks.md:
Plain idea: instead of one big program, Chromium runs many cooperating processes, each with only the rights its job needs. Early browsers ran everything in one process, so [one misbehaving page or plug-in could crash every tab](https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/multi-process-architecture/). Chromium's multi-process architecture fixed stability first; the same walls then limit what a compromised renderer can reach.

Tiny example: open three tabs on three sites. Your operating system's process list now shows one browser process, a GPU process, a few utility processes and (at least) three renderers. Each one was launched at the browser process's request, with a command line that says what it is.

The main roles, from Chromium's design documents:

- **Browser process**: runs the user interface (address bar, tabs, downloads) and manages all other processes. For each renderer it keeps a `RenderProcessHost`, and for each document a `RenderFrameHost`: browser-side objects that hold the trusted state about that renderer and frame.
- **Renderer processes**: run Blink (Chromium's rendering engine) and V8 for web content. They are sandboxed; their network access goes through the network service, and their access to files, display and input is restricted.
- **GPU process**: talks to graphics drivers for every renderer.
- **Network service**: does the HTTP, cookies and caching work, usually in its own utility process.
- **Utility processes**: everything else that can be split out, such as audio or decoding untrusted data. Chrome calls this direction [servicification](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/inside-browser-part1): each part of the browser runs as a service that can live in its own process, or be combined on low-memory devices.

blocks.title: Who talks to whom in Chromium

nodes.label:
Browser process
UI, policy, trusted state

scenes.caption: The browser process starts everything and keeps the trusted state about each child process.
Renderers run page code. They reach the outside world only by asking: the browser for permissions and navigation, the network service for fetches, the GPU process for drawing.
The GPU process receives command streams from every renderer and must validate each command before it reaches a driver. One GPU process serves many sites, which makes it a tempting escape target.
Utility processes such as the network and audio services run with their own sandbox types, tighter or looser depending on what the job needs.

blocks.md:
**Sandbox types.** Each child process is launched with a named sandbox type. Chromium's [sandbox type list](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/sandbox/policy/mojom/sandbox.mojom) has over 30 entries; a few matter here:

- `kRenderer`: hosts untrustworthy web content and blocks as much operating-system access as possible (it still allows dynamic code, which a JIT needs).
- `kService`: "computation only" services with very limited OS access; the preferred choice when it works.
- `kUtility`: generic utilities, which may be less locked down than `kService` on some platforms.
- `kGpu`: hosts the GPU service, which must talk to drivers and other OS interfaces.
- `kNetwork`: the network service. Its sandbox may be disabled by policy.
- `kNoSandbox`: runs with the same rights as the browser; the list says it is usually needed for stability, to host code that interacts with third-party code in another process.

The lesson: "sandboxed" is not one level. A renderer is far more locked down than the GPU or network process, which is why bugs in those processes count as escapes.

**The GPU process as a boundary.** Chromium's [command buffer design](https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/gpu-command-buffer/) has a renderer write graphics commands into shared memory and tell the GPU process where they end; the GPU process then checks each command, its arguments and whether they fit the current graphics state before calling the real driver. Its rule for developers: assume the client can go rogue, and never design a command that requires the client to be well behaved.

**Seeing the processes as a defender.** Every child is started with `--type=` on its command line: `renderer`, `gpu-process`, or `utility` plus a `--utility-sub-type=` naming the service and a `--service-sandbox-type=`. Most of these switch names are defined in Chromium's [content switches](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/content/public/common/content_switches.cc); a network service helper's command line carries, for example, `--utility-sub-type=network.mojom.NetworkService --service-sandbox-type=network`. Endpoint tools record the same command lines.

blocks.code:
# Classify Chromium child processes from command lines (synthetic
# listing; the switch names are real Chromium switches).
import re

LISTING = """\
101 1 /Applications/Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Chrome
102 101 Chrome Helper (GPU) --type=gpu-process --seatbelt-client=31
103 101 Chrome Helper --type=utility --utility-sub-type=network.mojom.NetworkService --service-sandbox-type=network
104 101 Chrome Helper --type=utility --utility-sub-type=audio.mojom.AudioService --service-sandbox-type=audio
105 101 Chrome Helper (Renderer) --type=renderer --renderer-client-id=7
106 101 Chrome Helper (Renderer) --type=renderer --renderer-client-id=9
107 105 /bin/zsh"""

procs = {}
for line in LISTING.splitlines():
    pid, ppid, cmd = line.split(" ", 2)
    m = re.search(r"--type=(\S+)", cmd)
    kind = m.group(1) if m else ("browser" if "Chrome" in cmd else "other")
    sub = re.search(r"--utility-sub-type=(\S+)", cmd)
    if sub:
        kind += ":" + sub.group(1).split(".")[0]
    procs[pid] = (ppid, kind)
    print(f"pid {pid:>3}  parent {ppid:>3}  {kind}")

for pid, (ppid, kind) in procs.items():
    parent = procs.get(ppid, (None, ""))[1]
    if kind == "other" and parent != "browser":
        print(f"ALERT: pid {pid} ({kind}) started by a {parent} process")
blocks.caption: Classifies a synthetic process listing by Chromium's --type switch and flags a non-browser child of a renderer.

pid 101  parent   1  browser
pid 102  parent 101  gpu-process
pid 103  parent 101  utility:network
pid 104  parent 101  utility:audio
pid 105  parent 101  renderer
pid 106  parent 101  renderer
pid 107  parent 105  other
ALERT: pid 107 (other) started by a renderer process

blocks.md: A sandboxed renderer should never be the parent of a shell or any other ordinary program. A process tree where a renderer (or the GPU or network process) starts something new is one of the clearest endpoint signals that a sandbox has failed.

blocks.question: Why is a bug in the GPU process treated as a possible sandbox escape, while the same bug class in a renderer is not?
options: The GPU process runs JavaScript
The GPU process has no IPC
GPU bugs cannot be patched
The GPU process runs with a looser sandbox, serves many renderers and talks to drivers, so reaching code there gets an attacker out of the renderer's tighter box
blocks.explain: Renderers get the tightest sandbox type. The GPU process needs driver and OS access, so code execution there is a step outside the renderer's jail. That is why the command buffer validates every command from a client it assumes may go rogue.

blocks.question: On an EDR (endpoint detection and response: security software that records process and file activity on each computer) console you see the process tree: Chrome browser process, then a Chrome Helper with `--type=renderer`, then `/bin/zsh`. What is the best reading?
options: Normal: renderers often open shells to run scripts
A likely renderer compromise plus sandbox failure; treat it as an incident
A network service crash
Normal for extensions
blocks.explain: Renderers ask the browser process for everything; they do not start ordinary programs. A shell under a renderer means the sandbox did not hold, either through a sandbox escape or a misconfiguration, and deserves incident handling.

lessons.title: Firefox Fission and WebKit: the same idea, different shapes

blocks.md:
Plain idea: all three major engines (Chromium's Blink, Mozilla's Gecko, Apple's WebKit) converged on the same design: a privileged parent process plus sandboxed content processes. They differ in how finely they split content, and that difference decides what a compromised content process can read.

Tiny example, from Mozilla's [Project Fission page](https://wiki.mozilla.org/Project_Fission): a blog on `example.com` embeds a Facebook like button and a Twitter button, each in a frame. Without site isolation the whole page, frames included, runs in one process, so a Firefox bug that lets the blog reach into the frames lets its owner act as the user on Facebook and Twitter. With site isolation the page runs in three sandboxed processes, one per site.

**Firefox and Fission.** *Fission* is Mozilla's name for its site isolation project: pages and frames run in processes dedicated to their site. Before it, Firefox already split content into several sandboxed content processes, but unrelated sites could share one. The [Firefox 95 release notes](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/95.0/releasenotes/) (December 2021) record that, to protect users against side-channel attacks such as Spectre, site isolation was enabled for all Firefox 95 users, which matches what you recalled from **The browser security model**.

Firefox names each content process by a **remoteType**. Its [process model documentation](https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/dom/ipc/process_model.html) lists, among others:

blocks.code:
# Group Firefox content processes by remoteType (synthetic list; the
# remoteType formats come from Firefox's process model documentation).
remote_types = [
    "webIsolated=https://bank.example",
    "webIsolated=https://news.example",
    "webIsolated=https://ads.example",
    "webCOOP+COEP=https://editor.example",
    "extension",
    "file",
    "web",
]
for rt in remote_types:
    kind, _, site = rt.partition("=")
    if kind == "webIsolated":
        note = "one site per process (Fission)"
    elif kind == "webCOOP+COEP":
        note = "cross-origin isolated: may use SharedArrayBuffer"
    elif kind == "file":
        note = "file:// pages, weaker sandbox than web content"
    elif kind == "web":
        note = "shared web content, not isolated"
    else:
        note = "elevated extension APIs"
    print(f"{kind:13} {site or '-':28} {note}")
blocks.caption: Reads remoteType strings in the documented formats. The list itself is synthetic.

webIsolated   https://news.example         one site per process (Fission)
webIsolated   https://ads.example          one site per process (Fission)
webCOOP+COEP  https://editor.example       cross-origin isolated: may use SharedArrayBuffer
extension     -                            elevated extension APIs

web           -                            shared web content, not isolated

blocks.md:
**WebKit.** WebKit's [architecture documentation](https://docs.webkit.org/Deep%20Dive/Architecture/WebKit2.html) describes a UI process (the app), one **WebContent** process per web page, and a shared **network process** that does network access, the disk cache and storage APIs such as IndexedDB. WebContent processes are "tightly sandboxed" because they JIT-compile JavaScript from the internet: no file system access unless the user grants it, no direct clipboard, microphone or camera; the UI process mediates those requests.

Note the unit: *per page*, not per site. WebKit's [site isolation document](https://docs.webkit.org/Deep%20Dive/SiteIsolation.html) defines a site as protocol plus registrable domain, and represents a cross-site frame living in another process as a `RemoteFrame`. As of January 2025 the document described the project as being on step 2 of 3 (fixing what the split breaks; step 3 is performance). It does not say the feature is on by default, so do not assume a cross-site iframe in Safari has its own process.

blocks.title: How much of the web gets its own process, by platform

scenes.caption: Chromium's own table: desktop Chrome isolates every site; Chrome for Android isolates some sites (logins and similar) on devices with about 2 GB of RAM or more.
Chromium's documentation lists low-memory Android, Android WebView and Chrome for iOS (built on WebKit) with no site isolation at all. Apps that embed a WebView inherit that.
Desktop Firefox isolates every site with Fission (on for all users since Firefox 95). WebKit's site isolation is documented as work in progress, so it is shown as not shipped by default.

blocks.md: Misconception: "every modern browser isolates every site." Coverage depends on product and device. Android WebView and low-memory Android have no site isolation in Chromium's documentation, and WebKit's is still being built. A risk assessment for an app that embeds web content must check the actual engine and platform.

blocks.question: In Mozilla's Fission example, a blog embeds Facebook and Twitter frames. Without site isolation, what is the risk if a Firefox bug lets page code read its own process's memory?
options: None: frames are always separate processes
The blog's code shares a process with the Facebook and Twitter frames, so it may read their data or act as the user in them
Only the blog's own cookies are exposed
The parent process crashes
blocks.explain: Without Fission the page and its cross-site frames run in one process, so a bug (or a Spectre-style read) in that process crosses sites. With Fission each site gets its own sandboxed process and that data is simply not there.

blocks.question: A mobile banking app shows its login page in an embedded Android WebView next to third-party ad frames. What does Chromium's process model documentation say about site isolation there?
options: Full site isolation, the same as desktop Chrome
Isolation only for login pages
No site isolation for Android WebView
Isolation only on devices with 8 GB of RAM
blocks.explain: The documentation lists Android WebView among the configurations with no site isolation. Defence there has to come from not mixing untrusted content with sensitive content in the same WebView and from keeping the WebView provider updated.

lessons.title: Site isolation in depth: process locks, jail and citadel checks

blocks.md:
Plain idea: site isolation is two promises. First, a process only ever **holds** documents from one site. Second, the browser process only ever **gives** that process data belonging to that site, even if the process lies about who it is. The first promise defeats reading memory you share; the second defeats asking for memory you do not.

Tiny example: a renderer for `ads.example` is compromised. Under the first promise, `bank.example` pages are not in its memory at all. Under the second, when it asks the browser for `bank.example`'s cookies, the browser checks which site that process is locked to and refuses.

**Why Spectre forced it.** Spectre (2018) let ordinary code infer memory in its own process through the CPU's speculative execution; the mechanics are taught in **Side channels and hardware security** (lesson "Spectre variant 1: speculating past a bounds check"). Ben Titzer and Jaroslav Sevcik of the V8 team wrote in [A year with Spectre](https://v8.dev/blog/spectre) (April 2019) that mitigating every Spectre leak in software was infeasible: putting speculation barriers (such as Intel's LFENCE) on every critical branch and retpolines (*return trampolines* that keep indirect branches from being speculated) on indirect branches made code 2 to 3 times slower on the Octane JavaScript benchmark. Their conclusion: "The only effective mitigation is to move sensitive data out of the process's address space." Meanwhile Chrome cut `performance.now()` resolution from 5 to 100 microseconds and added jitter, and browser vendors switched off `SharedArrayBuffer`, which returned only for cross-origin isolated pages (the COOP and COEP headers you met in the prerequisite).

**What a site is.** Chromium's [process model document](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/process_model_and_site_isolation.md) defines a site as scheme plus **eTLD+1**: the effective top-level domain plus one more label. The effective TLD comes from the [Public Suffix List](https://publicsuffix.org/), an initiative of Mozilla listing suffixes under which anyone can register names, such as `com`, `co.uk` and `github.io`. So `login.news.co.uk` and `news.co.uk` are one site, while `alice.github.io` and `bob.github.io` are two, and `http://news.co.uk` differs from `https://news.co.uk`.

**Process locks.** When a renderer is assigned a site, the browser records a **ProcessLock** for it; locks can be per site, per origin, per scheme (for example `file://`) or "allow any site" where isolation is off. Once a site lock is set it lasts for the life of that process host. A cross-site iframe gets its own process too: an **out-of-process iframe** (OOPIF).

blocks.code:
# Toy site isolation: site = scheme + eTLD+1, one locked process per site
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

PUBLIC_SUFFIXES = {"com", "example", "co.uk", "github.io"}  # tiny toy list

def site_of(url):
    u = urlsplit(url)
    labels = u.hostname.split(".")
    for i in range(len(labels)):            # longest suffix wins
        if ".".join(labels[i:]) in PUBLIC_SUFFIXES:
            return f"{u.scheme}://" + ".".join(labels[max(i - 1, 0):])
    return f"{u.scheme}://{u.hostname}"

locks = {}                                   # process id -> site lock
def process_for(url):
    site = site_of(url)
    for pid, lock in locks.items():
        if lock == site:
            return pid
    pid = 100 + len(locks)
    locks[pid] = site
    return pid

frames = ["https://news.co.uk/today", "https://ads.example/banner",
          "https://login.news.co.uk/", "https://alice.github.io/",
          "https://bob.github.io/", "http://news.co.uk/old"]
for url in frames:
    print(f"{url:28} site {site_of(url):24} process {process_for(url)}")

def can_access_data_for(pid, url):           # the browser-side "jail" check
    return locks.get(pid) == site_of(url)

print("renderer 101 asks for news.co.uk cookies:",
      can_access_data_for(101, "https://news.co.uk/"))

blocks.md:
**Enforcement in the browser process.** The same document describes two kinds of browser-side check on what a renderer asks for (for example in `ChildProcessSecurityPolicy::CanAccessDataForOrigin`):

- **Jail checks**: a process locked to a site may only access data belonging to that site. If every process is locked, this is enough.
- **Citadel checks**: an *unlocked* process may not access data for sites that require a dedicated process. This matters where full isolation is not available, such as Android, where only some sites get locked processes.

Plus **network response limits**: a locked renderer receives sensitive response types (HTML, XML, JSON) only from its own site, using CORB (Cross-Origin Read Blocking) or its successor ORB (Opaque Response Blocking, recalled from the prerequisite), while images and media still load cross-site.

blocks.title: A compromised ads renderer meets the jail check

scenes.caption: Normal case: the news renderer asks for its own cookies. The browser looks up the lock it set when it created that process, not anything the renderer says.
The ads renderer is compromised and asks for bank cookies. Its lock says ads.example, so the jail check fails.
A lying renderer is evidence of compromise, so the browser does not just refuse: it terminates the process (a bad-message kill).
A fresh ads renderer fetches bank JSON directly. The network service sees a JSON response for another site and withholds the body (ORB), so it never enters that process.

blocks.md:
**What it costs, and where it stops.** Chromium's [site isolation page](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/site-isolation/) reports about 10 to 13% more memory on desktop when isolating all sites with many tabs (Chrome 67), and 3 to 5% on Android when isolating sites users log into (Chrome 77). Because processes cost memory, desktop Chrome has a soft process limit; above it Chromium tries to reuse a process *of the same site*, never mixing sites in a locked process. Charles Reis, Alexander Moshchuk and Nasko Oskov of Google describe the design in [their USENIX Security 2019 paper](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity19/presentation/reis), which says it "locks each renderer process to documents from a single site".

Defenders can see it: `chrome://process-internals` shows whether a Site Isolation mode is on and how documents map to processes. Enterprises can force it with the `SitePerProcess` or `IsolateOrigins` policies; when a policy enables it, users cannot turn it off.

Site isolation keeps other sites' data out of a compromised renderer and refuses its forged requests. It does not stop that renderer from attacking the browser process through the IPC it is allowed to use. That boundary is the next two lessons.

blocks.question: Which pair of URLs would Chromium put in the same site, and so possibly the same locked process?
options: https://login.news.co.uk and https://news.co.uk
https://alice.github.io and https://bob.github.io
http://news.co.uk and https://news.co.uk
https://news.co.uk and https://news.com
blocks.explain: Site is scheme plus eTLD+1. co.uk is a public suffix, so news.co.uk is the registrable part and login.news.co.uk shares it. github.io is itself a public suffix, so alice and bob are different sites; a different scheme or TLD is also a different site.

blocks.question: Android Chrome locks only some sites to dedicated processes. Which check stops an unlocked renderer from asking for cookies of a site that should have a dedicated process?
options: The jail check
Opaque Response Blocking
The same-origin policy inside the renderer
The citadel check
blocks.explain: Jail checks constrain locked processes to their own site. Citadel checks constrain unlocked processes from touching sites that require isolation, which is exactly the partial-isolation case. ORB limits network responses, and in-renderer SOP checks are what a compromised renderer bypasses.

blocks.question: Why did the V8 team conclude that site isolation, not compiler changes, was the real Spectre defence?
options: Software mitigation of every possible Spectre leak was infeasible and costly, so the only effective fix was to keep sensitive data out of the attacker's address space
Compiler barriers were too hard to write
Spectre only affects the browser process
Site isolation also fixes the CPU
blocks.explain: Titzer and Sevcik found full software mitigation infeasible, with barriers costing 2 to 3 times on Octane. If another site's data is not in the process, there is nothing for a speculative read to find.

lessons.title: IPC and Mojo: the renderer asks, the browser decides

blocks.md:
Plain idea: a sandboxed renderer can do almost nothing on its own, so it sends requests to more privileged processes: "store this cookie", "open a file picker", "start a download". Each request arrives as a message, and the receiving code must treat every field in it as written by an attacker, because after a renderer bug it is.

Tiny example: a storage service in the browser process offers `read(origin)`. If it reads whatever origin the renderer names, a compromised renderer for `evil.example` simply asks for `bank.example`. Site isolation kept bank data out of the renderer's memory; this one parameter hands it back over IPC.

**IPC** (inter-process communication) is any way for processes to exchange data. Chromium's modern IPC system is **Mojo**, which its [README](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/mojo/README.md) describes as runtime libraries providing a platform-neutral abstraction of IPC primitives, a message IDL format and a bindings library. The pieces:

- A **message pipe** is a two-ended channel; messages written at one end arrive at the other. Pipes can also carry operating-system **handles** (references to kernel objects such as open files) from one process to another.
- **Mojom** is Mojo's IDL (interface definition language): a file declares an interface and its methods, and code generators produce bindings for C++, JavaScript, Java and Rust.
- A `mojo::Remote` is the calling end of an interface and a `mojo::Receiver` the implementing end.

Each frame gets a `BrowserInterfaceBroker` through which it requests browser interfaces, and Chromium's [Mojo security guidance](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/mojo.md) notes that each such broker is strongly associated with an origin. Underneath Mojo, Chrome now uses a library called [ipcz](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/third_party/ipcz/README.md), integrated directly into Mojo's core, to move the messages.

The guidance turns the trust rule into design rules:

- "Do not trust less privileged processes": treat their data as if a malicious adversary generated it, and validate on the more privileged side.
- The browser "must not (fully) trust the renderer's claims about origins"; it already knows which origin a frame has committed (`RenderFrameHost::GetLastCommittedOrigin()`). A method that needs the renderer to send its own origin "has a conceptual error".
- If an origin must cross IPC anyway, check it with `ChildProcessSecurityPolicy` (the jail and citadel checks from lesson 4) and, if it fails, reject the message with `mojo::ReportBadMessage()`, which terminates the renderer. It "does not stop execution of the current function", so the code must `return` right after.
- Use specific types: `url.mojom.Origin` rather than a URL, and certainly not a string; an interface rather than a raw pipe; `mojo_base.mojom.File` rather than a raw descriptor.
- "Policy should be controlled solely by the browser process."

scenes.caption: The browser created this host for a renderer locked to evil.example and stored that fact in the host object.
Vulnerable design: the method takes an origin argument and believes it. A compromised renderer names bank.example and gets bank data.
Fixed design: the method takes no origin. The host uses the lock it already holds, so the renderer can only ever read its own data.
Checked design: an origin arrives, does not match the lock, and the host reports a bad message. The browser kills the lying renderer.

blocks.md:
Chromium's older [security tips for IPC](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/education/security-tips-for-ipc/) add traps that still apply to Mojo:

- `DCHECK` (debug check) is compiled out of release builds, so using it to validate renderer input gives "a false sense of security". Lesson 6 shows a real escape with exactly this shape.
- Do not use `CHECK` (which crashes the browser) on untrusted input either; ignore it or disconnect the sender.
- Prefer allowlists and narrow types (enums, integer IDs) over strings.
- Send limited capabilities (an already-opened read-only file) rather than letting the renderer name a path for the browser to open.
- Never send pointers, and assume IDs can be spoofed: a compromised process can name another valid ID that belongs to someone else.

Ask of every IPC method: which argument identifies *who is asking*, and does the privileged side get that from its own state or from the message? Identity must come from the browser's state. Everything in the message is attacker input to be range-checked, type-checked and allowlisted.

Defender view: a renderer killed by `ReportBadMessage` disappears like a crashed renderer (the user sees a crashed tab). A cluster of such terminations on one site in your crash telemetry is worth a look, because honest renderers do not send impossible messages.

blocks.question: A new Mojo method is proposed: `SetPermission(url.mojom.Origin origin, bool allowed)`, called by the renderer for its frame. What is the core problem?
options: It should use a string instead of url.mojom.Origin
Booleans cannot cross Mojo
It lets the renderer name the origin whose permission changes; the browser should use the frame's committed origin from its own state
It needs a DCHECK on the origin
blocks.explain: Mojo's guidance says a method that needs the renderer to send its origin has a conceptual error. The browser already knows the frame's committed origin. A string would be worse, and a DCHECK vanishes in release builds.

blocks.question: A browser-side handler finds that a renderer sent an origin it is not allowed to access. It calls `mojo::ReportBadMessage()`. What must the next line be?
options: Nothing: ReportBadMessage stops the function
A return, because ReportBadMessage does not stop execution of the current function
A CHECK to crash the browser
A retry of the request
blocks.explain: The guidance stresses that ReportBadMessage does not stop the current function. Without an immediate return, the handler would go on to perform the forbidden action anyway. CHECK on untrusted input would crash the browser instead of the renderer.

lessons.title: Sandbox escapes at the IPC boundary: CVE-2025-2783 and CVE-2020-16010

blocks.md:
Plain idea: a sandbox escape does not need a memory bug in the sandbox. It needs the privileged side to do something powerful on behalf of the sandboxed side that it should have refused. Two in-the-wild Chrome escapes show the two common shapes: a logic error in what the broker hands back, and a memory bug in how the broker processes data the renderer sent.

Background term: on Windows a **handle** is a number that refers to an object the kernel manages for a process (a file, a thread, another process). `DuplicateHandle` copies a handle from one process into another. Windows also has **pseudo handles**: special constants returned by `GetCurrentProcess()` (-1) and `GetCurrentThread()` (-2) that the kernel interprets as "the calling process" or "the calling thread".

**CVE-2025-2783 (March 2025).** The security company Kaspersky detected a wave of infections in mid-March 2025 and named it [Operation ForumTroll](https://securelist.com/operation-forumtroll/115989/): personalised, short-lived links in phishing emails inviting recipients to the "Primakov Readings" forum, sent to media outlets, educational institutions and government organisations in Russia. Opening the link in Chrome was enough. Kaspersky captured the sandbox escape; the renderer exploit that should have preceded it was not obtained. Boris Larin and Igor Kuznetsov of Kaspersky reported it on 20 March, and [Chrome 134.0.6998.177/.178 for Windows](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2025/03/stable-channel-update-for-desktop_25.html) fixed it on 25 March as "Incorrect handle provided in unspecified circumstances in Mojo on Windows", noting an exploit existed in the wild.

Kaspersky's later Securelist write-up, "Mem3nt0 mori: The Hacking Team is back!" (27 October 2025; cited by name and not linked, because it walks through the exploit's steps), gives the root cause: Chrome's IPC code already rejected the pseudo handle -1, but not -2. When the broker passed a -2 received from the renderer to `DuplicateHandle`, the kernel read it as the broker's own current thread, so the renderer was handed a real handle to a thread in the privileged process.

blocks.title: How a pseudo handle turned into the broker's own thread

scenes.caption: Normal relay: the renderer sends handle 4, a file it owns. The broker duplicates it and the kernel resolves it in the renderer's table.
The broker rejects -1, the known pseudo handle for 'current process'.
But -2 means 'current thread', and the kernel resolves pseudo handles relative to the caller: the broker. The renderer receives a real handle to a broker thread.
Fix shape: accept only handles that exist in the sender's own handle set, and report any other value as a bad message.

blocks.md: **One bug, two browsers.** Two days later Mozilla shipped [Firefox 136.0.4 (MFSA 2025-19, a Mozilla Foundation Security Advisory)](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2025-19/): after the Chrome escape, Firefox developers "identified a similar pattern in our IPC code", where a compromised child process could make the parent return "an unintentionally powerful handle". It was CVE-2025-2857, Windows only. That is **variant analysis**: when a bug class is published, look for the same pattern in your own code. Kaspersky later linked the toolset to Dante, commercial spyware from the Italian company Memento Labs (formerly Hacking Team, a vendor of surveillance software to governments), and called the pattern a whole class "worth hunting for" in other software. Its stated lesson: if a privileged process accepts a handle from a less privileged one, it must return an error for any pseudo handle.

**CVE-2020-16010 (November 2020).** [Chrome 86.0.4240.185 for Android](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2020/11/chrome-for-android-update.html) fixed a heap buffer overflow in UI on Android, reported by Maddie Stone, Mark Brand and Sergei Glazunov of Project Zero (Google's vulnerability research team) and exploited in the wild. Project Zero's [root-cause analysis](https://googleprojectzero.github.io/0days-in-the-wild/0day-RCAs/2020/CVE-2020-16010.html) explains it: browser-side code converting a Skia bitmap (Skia is Chrome's 2D graphics library) into an Android Java bitmap handled only some pixel formats. For an unsupported one it hit `NOTREACHED()`, which then "has no effect in release builds" (it now crashes), and fell back to 32 bits per pixel. A renderer-supplied bitmap in a 64-bit-per-pixel format then got a destination buffer half the size of its pixels, and the copy used the input size. The analysis says to check every input parameter before converting and to check the destination size before the copy. It was chained with a renderer bug, CVE-2020-15999 (lesson 10).

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow l6_bitmap.c:19 in convert_vulnerable

blocks.md: Defender view for both cases: patch within days (CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, put CVE-2025-2783 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 27 March 2025 with a 21-day deadline), inventory every Chromium-based browser and Electron app (apps that embed Chromium; lesson 12), and alert on a browser child process loading unexpected DLLs or starting programs. Kaspersky's October 2025 write-up cites a rule for a DLL load in a Chrome process started from Outlook.

blocks.question: In the CVE-2025-2783 pattern, why did checking only for -1 fail?
options: -1 is a valid handle on Windows
Mojo encrypts handles
The renderer could not send negative numbers
Windows has other pseudo handles, including -2 for the current thread, and the kernel resolves them relative to the process that calls DuplicateHandle, which was the broker
blocks.explain: Kaspersky's analysis: GetCurrentThread returns -2, there was no check for -2 or other undocumented pseudo handles, and DuplicateHandle in the broker turned it into a real handle to the broker's own thread. A denylist of one value missed the class; an allowlist of the sender's real handles does not.

blocks.question: The CVE-2020-16010 code had a debug-only assertion for unsupported formats. What made that insufficient?
options: Assertions are slow
The assertion was in Java
The renderer could disable assertions
Debug-only checks (DCHECK, assert, and NOTREACHED as it worked in 2020) do nothing in release builds, so release code silently took the fallback path
blocks.explain: Project Zero noted that NOTREACHED had no effect in release builds at the time (Chromium has since made it crash in every build), the same trap Chromium's IPC tips warn about for DCHECK. Validation of data from a less privileged process must be a real runtime check that rejects the input.

lessons.title: JavaScript engines: tiers, shapes and stale assumptions

blocks.md:
Plain idea: a JavaScript engine is a compiler that takes its input from strangers and has to guess the types of everything to run fast. When a guess or a cached decision stays in use after the page has changed the facts, the engine reads one kind of value as another. That is a **type confusion**. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (November 2026 edition) lists 41 V8 entries, 20 of them named as type confusions.

Tiny example: the engine decides "property `a` lives in slot 0" and is about to write there. Before it writes, page script runs and moves `a` to slot 1. The engine writes slot 0 anyway, over whatever lives there now.

**Tiers.** V8 runs code in stages, according to the [Maglev announcement](https://v8.dev/blog/maglev) (December 2023): every function is first compiled to bytecode and run by **Ignition**, the interpreter; hot functions are turned into machine code by **Sparkplug**, a fast baseline compiler added in 2021; hotter ones by **Maglev**, an optimizing compiler that produces "good enough code, fast enough" (shipped in Chrome M117); and the hottest by **TurboFan**, the optimizing compiler aimed at peak speed. A **JIT** (just-in-time) compiler is one that generates machine code while the program runs, just before it is needed.

**Shapes.** JavaScript objects behave like dictionaries, but V8 gives every object a **hidden class** describing its shape. [V8's write-up on fast properties](https://v8.dev/blog/fast-properties) explains that the hidden class maps property names to their positions in the object, giving the engine a fast way to identify an object's shape; objects built the same way share one. Optimized code checks the hidden class once and then reads fields at fixed offsets. Every such check is an assumption the engine must keep true or throw away.

**CVE-2021-30551 (June 2021).** Google's Threat Analysis Group (TAG) found this V8 type confusion exploited on Chrome 91.0.4472.77; [Chrome 91.0.4472.101](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2021/06/stable-channel-update-for-desktop.html) fixed it on 9 June 2021. TAG's [account of the campaign](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/how-we-protect-users-0-day-attacks/) says targets were believed to be in Armenia and received one-time links by email; the attackers fingerprinted each visitor before deciding to deliver the exploit. TAG assessed that a commercial surveillance vendor built and sold the exploits, and Citizen Lab (a research lab at the University of Toronto's Munk School) later tied the activity to the spyware vendor Candiru.

Root cause, from Project Zero's analysis by Sergei Glazunov (not linked here because the page includes trigger code): a DOM object type, `HTMLEmbedElement`, has a property *interceptor*, a hook that runs on property access and can run page JavaScript. During a property store V8 consulted the interceptor, the page's script defined the same property on the object meanwhile, and V8 then added a *second* property with that name, leaving the object corrupted. The fix, V8 commit [Fix handling of interceptors](https://chromium.googlesource.com/v8/v8/+/f9857fdf743eeb263aec3944259ad811f564291b) by Igor Sheludko, restarts the lookup after the interceptor so changes made by user code are seen.

blocks.title: A toy store whose decision goes stale
blocks.code:
o.shape = {"a": (0, "num"), "b": (1, "obj")}
o.slots = [0x7, 0x1000]          # b points at an Array

def relayout(o):                 # page code, run mid-store
    o.shape = {"b": (0, "obj"), "a": (1, "num")}
    o.slots = [o.slots[1], o.slots[0]]

def store(o, name, raw, kind, callback):
    slot, k = o.shape[name]      # decide where to write
    if k != kind:
        raise TypeError("kind mismatch")
    callback(o)                  # user code runs here
    o.slots[slot] = raw          # BUG: slot may be stale

store(o, "a", 0x2000, "num", relayout)
slot, kind = o.shape["b"]        # optimized load of o.b
value = HEAP[o.slots[slot]]      # trusts kind == "obj"

scenes.caption: The object's shape (its hidden class, in the toy a dict) says a is a number in slot 0 and b is an object reference in slot 1, pointing at an Array.
store looks up a: slot 0, kind num. The kind check passes. The decision 'write slot 0' is now made.
Page code runs in the middle of the store (in V8's case, an interceptor). It swaps the layout: b now lives in slot 0.
The store writes the number 0x2000 into slot 0, which the shape now says holds b, an object reference.
Optimized code loads b, sees kind obj, and treats 0x2000 as an object address. A number the page chose is now read as an object: type confusion.
scenes.output: recheck=False slots=['0x2000', '0x7'] b -> another object's bytes

scenes.caption: With the fix (the recheck in the full toy below), the lookup is redone after the callback, as V8's patch restarts its lookup. The write lands in a's new slot and b still points at the Array.

blocks.caption: The full toy, with the fix as a recheck flag. Toy model: real engines use maps, descriptors and compiled code, not Python dicts.

blocks.code:
recheck=False slots=['0x2000', '0x7'] b -> another object's bytes
recheck=True  slots=['0x1000', '0x2000'] b -> Array(len=2)
blocks.caption: Output of python3 l7_interp.py.

blocks.md: The recurring root cause: the engine makes a decision (a slot, a type, "this check is redundant"), then lets user JavaScript run (a getter, a setter, an interceptor, a valueOf call), then acts on the old decision. Fixes either re-validate after any point where user code can run, or make that point impossible.

Misconception: "rewrite the engine in a memory-safe language and this goes away." The V8 sandbox post points out that when a compiler is part of the attack surface, a memory-safe implementation language cannot guarantee the code it *generates* is safe. That is why V8 adds containment (lesson 9) instead of relying on the language alone.

blocks.question: In the toy, which change fixes the bug without slowing every store by much?
options: Look the property up again after the callback has run, and re-check its kind
Remove the kind check
Run the callback after the write
Make slots a tuple
blocks.explain: Re-validating after user code runs is the fix pattern the V8 patch follows. Running the callback after the write changes behaviour JavaScript relies on, and removing checks makes things worse.

blocks.question: Why is a V8 type confusion rated High rather than Critical by default?
options: V8 bugs cannot corrupt memory
Type confusions are never exploited
Code execution from it stays inside the sandboxed renderer unless another bug escapes
V8 runs in the browser process
blocks.explain: V8 runs in the renderer, so even a fully exploited type confusion gives code execution inside the sandbox, the guideline's High case. It becomes part of a Critical chain only with an escape like those in lesson 6.

lessons.title: Bounds-check elimination: when the optimizer proves the wrong thing

blocks.md:
Plain idea: checking `0 <= i < length` before every array access costs time, so optimizing compilers try to prove the check can never fail and delete it. The proof comes from **range analysis**: tracking the smallest and largest value each variable can hold. If the range analysis is wrong for one corner case, the compiler deletes a check that was needed, and an out-of-bounds read or write appears in the generated code even though the source was correct.

Tiny example: the compiler reasons "`abs(x)` is never negative, so `abs(x) >> 28` is between 0 and 7, and the array has 8 elements, so no check is needed." In 32-bit arithmetic `abs(-2147483648)` is still -2147483648, because +2147483648 does not fit. Shift it right by 28 and you get -8.

In TurboFan the range analysis is done by the **typer**, which assigns every value a type that includes a numeric range, and a later phase removed `CheckBounds` nodes whose index range was provably inside the array. That made typer mistakes valuable to attackers: one wrong range became a missing bounds check.

V8's response in February 2019 was a hardening change rather than a single bug fix. Jaroslav Sevcik's commit [Introduce aborting bounds checks](https://chromium.googlesource.com/v8/v8/+/7bb6dc0e06fa158df508bc8997f0fce4e33512a5) stopped eliminating bounds checks based on types; instead the compiler keeps an *aborting* bounds check that crashes the process rather than deoptimizing (falling back to slower code). A typer mistake now turns into a crash, a denial of service, instead of silent out-of-bounds access.

blocks.code:
# Toy optimizer: drop a bounds check when range analysis "proves" it.
def i32(x):                              # wrap to a 32-bit signed int
    x &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    return x - (1 << 32) if x & 0x80000000 else x

def abs32(x):                            # what 32-bit machine code does
    return i32(-x) if x < 0 else x

# Range analysis (the "typer"): abs32 returns [0, 2**31-1], so
# abs32(x) >> 28 is in [0, 7]. Wrong: abs32(-2**31) is still -2**31.
TYPER_RANGE = (0, 7)

MEMORY = ["neighbour"] * 8 + [f"a[{i}]" for i in range(8)]  # a starts at 8
A_BASE, A_LEN = 8, 8

def load(i, keep_check):
    lo, hi = TYPER_RANGE
    proven = 0 <= lo and hi < A_LEN      # compiler: check is redundant
    if keep_check or not proven:
        if not 0 <= i < A_LEN:
            return "abort: index out of bounds"
    return MEMORY[A_BASE + i]

for x in (5, 1 << 30, -(1 << 31)):
    i = abs32(x) >> 28                   # Python >> is arithmetic, like sar
    print(f"x={x:>11}  i={i:>2}  eliminated: {load(i, False):11}"
          f"  hardened: {load(i, True)}")
blocks.caption: A toy optimizer with a wrong range rule, run with the check eliminated and with a hardened aborting check. Memory is a flat list: a neighbouring object, then the 8-element array.

blocks.code:
x=          5  i= 0  eliminated: a[0]         hardened: a[0]
x= 1073741824  i= 4  eliminated: a[4]         hardened: a[4]
x=-2147483648  i=-8  eliminated: neighbour    hardened: abort: index out of bounds
blocks.caption: Output of python3 l8_bce.py.

scenes.caption: Memory in the toy: a neighbouring object in cells 0 to 7, the array a in cells 8 to 15. Index i is added to the array base, 8.
x = 5 gives i = 0: the access reads a[0]. With or without the check this is fine.
x = 2^30 gives i = 4: still inside, as the range analysis predicted.
x = -2^31: abs overflows and stays negative, i = -8. The check was eliminated, so base 8 plus -8 reads cell 0: the neighbour's data.
With the hardened aborting check the same index stops the program before any access. A typer bug becomes a crash instead of a read.

blocks.prompt: Hardening keeps the aborting check. Does that mean the wrong range rule in the typer no longer matters?
blocks.reveal: No. The wrong range is still a bug and still gets fixed. Other optimizations use the same range facts (for example to pick a faster integer operation or remove another check), so a bad range can still cause wrong behaviour elsewhere. Hardening limits the worst outcome of one known pattern. It is defence in depth, not a replacement for a correct typer, and Chromium's severity guideline lists "V8 correctness issues where different compiler tiers return different results" as Medium-severity bugs for that reason.

blocks.md:
**How these bugs get found.** Because each tier must compute the same result, a powerful test is **differential testing**: run the same JavaScript in the interpreter and in the optimizing tiers and flag any difference. That is why Chromium rates mismatches between tiers as security-relevant even when no memory corruption is shown. Fuzzers that generate JavaScript programs and compare tiers are covered in **Fuzzing and vulnerability research**.

**Defender view.** You will not see a bounds-check bug in logs; the defence is speed of patching and reducing JIT exposure where it is not needed (lesson 9 covers the JIT policy). Aborting checks and other hardening crash the renderer, so crash spikes for one site in crash telemetry can be the only trace of probing.
Optimizers turn proofs into deleted checks. When the proof can be wrong, keep a cheap check that crashes. A crash costs availability; a missing check costs memory safety.

blocks.question: Why is a bug in range analysis more dangerous in an optimizing JIT than in an ordinary static compiler?
options: JITs do not do range analysis
The JIT compiles attacker-written code on the victim's machine, so the attacker can write exactly the program that hits the wrong range and removes a needed check
Static compilers never remove bounds checks
JIT code runs in the kernel
blocks.explain: A static compiler's input is the developer's trusted source. A browser JIT's input is any page's JavaScript, so a single unsound rule becomes something an attacker can trigger on demand.

blocks.question: What does V8's 2019 'aborting bounds check' change trade?
options: A small run-time cost and possible crashes for the guarantee that a wrong type does not silently remove a bounds check
Memory safety for speed
Correctness for compatibility
Nothing: it only renamed a node
blocks.explain: The commit replaced type-based check elimination with a check that crashes instead of deoptimizing. That costs a little speed and turns typer bugs into crashes, but removes them as a silent route to out-of-bounds access.

lessons.title: Containing the engine: pointer cages, the V8 sandbox and JIT policy

blocks.md:
Plain idea: if V8 bugs will keep happening, make the memory a V8 bug can corrupt smaller. Instead of letting a corrupted field point anywhere in the process, store fields so that, however they are corrupted, they can only point into one reserved region. A bug then corrupts V8's own heap but cannot directly reach the rest of the renderer.

Tiny example: a field holds a full 64-bit address, and an attacker overwrites it with the address of some other library's data. If the field instead holds a 40-bit *offset* from a fixed base, the worst the attacker can write still lands inside the reserved region.

**Step 1: pointer compression.** Igor Sheludko and Santiago Aboy Solanes described it in [March 2020](https://v8.dev/blog/pointer-compression): V8 allocates all of a heap's objects inside one 4 GB region and stores pointers as 32-bit offsets from its base. It was done to save memory (V8 heap size down by up to 43%, renderer memory by up to 20% on desktop), but it created the idea of a **cage**: a region all heap references are relative to.

**Step 2: the V8 sandbox.** Samuel Gross's [April 2024 post](https://v8.dev/blog/sandbox) extends the idea to a 1 TB reserved region. Every field that could reach outside memory is replaced: pointers into the sandbox become 40-bit offsets from its base, and references to objects outside it (owned by Blink, for example) go through a **pointer table**, so in-sandbox data holds only an index. The V8 sandbox's [design notes](https://chromium.googlesource.com/v8/v8.git/+/refs/heads/main/src/sandbox/README.md) state the attacker model plainly: the attacker can arbitrarily and concurrently modify any memory inside the sandbox. Objects that must not be corrupted, such as bytecode containers and metadata for JIT code, are moved to a **trusted space** outside the sandbox and reached through another table indirection, with a dedicated **code pointer table** for machine-code pointers.

blocks.code:
# Toy V8-style sandbox: a 64 KiB region (real V8: 1 TB, 40-bit offsets).
SANDBOX_BASE = 0x7F0000000000
OFFSET_BITS = 16
SIZE = 1 << OFFSET_BITS

def decode_raw_pointer(field):            # before: field is a full address
    return field

def decode_sandboxed(field):              # after: field is an offset
    return SANDBOX_BASE + (field & (SIZE - 1))

# Pointers to objects outside the sandbox go through a table of
# (type tag, address); in-sandbox data holds only an index.
EXTERNAL_TABLE = [("FileHandle", 0x5551000), ("AudioBuffer", 0x5552000)]

def decode_external(index, expected_type):
    tag, addr = EXTERNAL_TABLE[index % len(EXTERNAL_TABLE)]
    if tag != expected_type:              # wrong tag: unusable pointer
        return addr | 0xFFFF000000000000  # faults if dereferenced
    return addr

corrupted = 0x00005551000             # attacker overwrote a field in the sandbox
print("raw pointer     ->", hex(decode_raw_pointer(corrupted)))
addr = decode_sandboxed(corrupted)
print("sandboxed offset->", hex(addr),
      "inside" if SANDBOX_BASE <= addr < SANDBOX_BASE + SIZE else "OUTSIDE")
print("external, right ->", hex(decode_external(1, "AudioBuffer")))
print("external, wrong ->", hex(decode_external(0, "AudioBuffer")))

blocks.title: One corrupted field, before and after the sandbox (simplified)

scenes.caption: Simplified address space: the V8 sandbox is a reserved block (SB), with Blink's heap, libraries, the external pointer table (EPT) and trusted space outside it.
Without the sandbox, a heap field holds a full address. After a V8 bug overwrites it, it can point at Blink's heap or a library: corruption spreads beyond V8.
With the sandbox, the same field is an offset from the sandbox base. Whatever value is written, base plus offset lands inside SB.
Objects outside the sandbox are reached by index through the EPT, whose entries carry a type tag. A swapped index with the wrong tag yields an invalid pointer that faults if used.
Bytecode containers and JIT metadata live in trusted space, outside the attacker-writable region. To escape, an attacker now needs a second bug: a sandbox bypass.

blocks.md:
**Does it hold?** The post reports an overhead of around 1% or less on typical workloads, says the sandbox had been on by default on 64-bit Chrome builds for about two years, and treats Chrome 123 as a kind of beta release of its security guarantees. The attacker model is testable: V8 can be built with `v8_enable_memory_corruption_api`, which emulates arbitrary read and write inside the sandbox, so researchers can try to escape without first finding a V8 bug. The sandbox entered Chrome's Vulnerability Reward Program, and Google's [2024 VRP review](https://blog.google/security/vulnerability-reward-program-2024-in/) records dedicated V8 Sandbox Bypass rewards launched that year.

The same table design appears in V8's source: each [external pointer table](https://chromium.googlesource.com/v8/v8.git/+/refs/heads/main/src/sandbox/external-pointer-table.h) entry stores the pointer together with a type tag, and if the tag the reader expects does not match, "the resulting pointer will be invalid and cannot be dereferenced".

**JIT policy: removing the compiler from the attack surface.** Recall W^X from **Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI**: a JIT must write machine code and then make it executable. V8 can also run with no JIT at all. The [jitless mode](https://v8.dev/blog/jitless) (V8 7.4, March 2019) allocates no executable memory at run time and interprets everything with Ignition. Its measured cost: Speedometer 2.0 about 40% slower and the Web Tooling Benchmark about 80% slower, but only about 6% slower JavaScript in a simulated YouTube TV session.

Chrome exposes this to administrators as the [`DefaultJavaScriptJitSetting`](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/policy/resources/templates/policy_definitions/ContentSettings/DefaultJavaScriptJitSetting.yaml) policy (since Chrome 93), with `JavaScriptJitAllowedForSites` and `JavaScriptJitBlockedForSites` for exceptions. Its description says disabling the JIT may make rendering slower and may disable parts of JavaScript including WebAssembly, and "may allow" Chrome to render content in a more secure configuration.

A practical pattern for high-risk users: block the JIT by default and allow it only for the business web apps that need speed. Every unknown site then runs through the interpreter, removing the optimizing compilers (where bugs like lesson 8's live) from what a drive-by page can reach.

blocks.question: An attacker has a V8 bug that lets them overwrite any field inside V8's heap. With the V8 sandbox on, what do they still need to corrupt memory outside it, such as Blink objects?
options: A second bug: a sandbox bypass, because in-sandbox fields are offsets or table indices that cannot name outside memory
Nothing: the sandbox only slows them down
Administrator rights
A Spectre gadget
blocks.explain: The sandbox's attacker model already assumes arbitrary writes inside it. Fields that point out are offsets or table indexes with type tags, so escaping requires a separate bypass bug, which Chrome's VRP pays for separately.

blocks.question: What does blocking the JavaScript JIT with enterprise policy trade?
options: Nothing: it is free
Site isolation for speed
Speed (large on JavaScript-heavy benchmarks) and possibly WebAssembly support, for a smaller attack surface
It disables JavaScript entirely
blocks.explain: The policy description says pages may render more slowly and parts of JavaScript including WebAssembly may be disabled. Jitless measurements show large benchmark slowdowns but small ones on lighter sites. JavaScript still runs, in the interpreter.

lessons.title: Memory safety strategy: the Rule of 2, MiraclePtr, Rust and RLBox

blocks.md:
Plain idea: you cannot fix memory bugs one at a time fast enough, so decide *where* memory-unsafe code is allowed to meet attacker data, and reduce how much such code there is. Chromium writes the first half down as a rule every new feature must pass.

Tiny example: a feature wants to decode PNG images sent by web pages, in C, inside the browser process. That is attacker input, an unsafe language and high privilege at once. Move the decoding into a sandboxed process, or use a memory-safe decoder, and one of the three goes away.

**The Rule of 2.** Chromium's [Rule of 2](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/rule-of-2.md) names three properties: untrustworthy inputs; an unsafe implementation language (one that lacks memory safety, including at least C, C++ and assembly); and high privilege. "Pick no more than 2." Ways to comply, from the document:

- **Lower the privilege**: launch a sandboxed utility process to handle the data. Its example: converting a PNG to Skia's bitmap type in a sandboxed process, so the high-privilege side only receives a simple, safe format (this is **normalisation**).
- **Use a safe language**: Rust for third-party libraries (its example is a QR code generator), Java on Android, Swift on iOS.
- **Trust the source**: data from a verified trusted source may be parsed at high privilege in an unsafe language.

The reason, from Chromium's [memory safety page](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/memory-safety/): of 912 high or critical security bugs affecting Stable since 2015, about 70% were memory-safety bugs, and half of those were use-after-free.

blocks.code:
# Rule of 2 review: untrustworthy input, unsafe language, high privilege.
# Pick no more than two. (Inventory is a made-up design review.)
components = [
    # name,                        untrusted, unsafe, privileged
    ("image decoder in renderer",   True,  True,  False),
    ("image decoder in browser",    True,  True,  True),
    ("font parser rewritten in Rust", True, False, False),
    ("settings page (browser UI)",  False, True,  True),
    ("JSON parser in Rust, browser", True,  False, True),
]
for name, untrusted, unsafe, privileged in components:
    n = untrusted + unsafe + privileged
    verdict = "VIOLATES Rule of 2" if n == 3 else "ok"
    fixes = []
    if n == 3:
        fixes = ["move to a sandboxed utility process",
                 "rewrite in a memory-safe language",
                 "normalise input in a sandbox first"]
    print(f"{name:31} {n}/3 {verdict}")
    for f in fixes:
        print(f"{'':35}- {f}")

blocks.md: **MiraclePtr.** Recall from **Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI**: MiraclePtr (BackupRefPtr) quarantines freed memory that raw pointers still refer to, turning many use-after-free bugs in the browser process into unexploitable ones. Chrome treats a way around it as a vulnerability in its own right: the 2024 VRP review lists a MiraclePtr Bypass Reward raised to USD 250,128, and the year's top Chrome award (USD 100,115) went to a MiraclePtr bypass.

**Fonts and Rust: a case for replacing a parser.** Fonts are programs as much as data: TrueType hinting and CFF charstrings need small virtual machines to run. CVE-2020-15999 was a heap overflow in FreeType, the font library Chrome used, fixed in [Chrome 86.0.4240.111](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2020/10/stable-channel-update-for-desktop_20.html) on 20 October 2020 after an in-the-wild report by Sergei Glazunov. Project Zero's [analysis](https://googleprojectzero.github.io/0days-in-the-wild/0day-RCAs/2020/CVE-2020-15999.html): `Load_SBit_Png` truncated an embedded PNG's width and height to 16 bits when sizing a buffer, but passed the full 32-bit values to libpng, so images wider or taller than 65535 overflowed it. It was chained with a Windows kernel bug and, on Android, with CVE-2020-16010 from lesson 6.

Chrome's answer was to replace FreeType for web fonts. Dominik Röttsches, Rod Sheeter and Chad Brokaw describe [Fontations](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/memory-safety-fonts) (March 2025), a family of Rust font libraries whose Skrifa component replaces the parts of FreeType Skia used. Keeping up with FreeType fuzzing findings cost at least a quarter of an engineer; fuzzing Skrifa had found 39 bugs, none security critical. Rollout: Chrome 128 for less common formats, Chrome 133 for all web fonts on Linux, Android and ChromeOS, system fonts on Linux and Android in Chrome 136, and FreeType removed from Blink in Chrome 145.

**RLBox: sandboxing inside the process.** Some components are too small or entangled for their own process. Mozilla's answer is RLBox, built with researchers from UC San Diego, Stanford and UT Austin and described in [Retrofitting Fine Grain Isolation in the Firefox Renderer](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity20/presentation/narayan) (USENIX Security 2020). A C library is compiled to WebAssembly, so it cannot touch memory outside its own region, and RLBox's C++ types make every crossing explicit. The paper sandboxes libjpeg, libpng, libtheora, libvpx, libvorbis and zlib in experiments, and reports the Graphite font-shaping library sandboxed this way in production Firefox; the [Firefox 95 release notes](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/95.0/releasenotes/) say RLBox was then enabled on all platforms. The [RLBox documentation](https://rlbox.dev/) states the rule: every value from the sandboxed library must be validated before Firefox uses it, because a compromised library could otherwise abuse Firefox code. RLBox enforces this by marking such values **tainted**.

Misconception: "a sandbox makes a memory bug harmless." It makes it worth less. A sandboxed decoder bug still gives code execution inside that sandbox, which is why Chromium still fixes and rewards such bugs as High, and why the Rule of 2 prefers removing the unsafe language when it can.

blocks.question: A team wants to parse a new image format sent by web pages, in C++, inside the browser process, to show a preview in the address bar. Which change does NOT satisfy the Rule of 2?
options: Decode in a sandboxed utility process and pass a simple bitmap to the browser
Use a memory-safe Rust decoder in the browser process
Only decode images from a verified trusted source
Keep it in the browser process but add extra fuzzing
blocks.explain: Fuzzing finds bugs but leaves all three properties in place: untrusted input, unsafe language, high privilege. The other options each remove one property: privilege, unsafe language, or untrusted input.

blocks.question: Why does RLBox mark values returned by a sandboxed library as tainted?
options: To speed up WebAssembly
Because the library may already be compromised, so its outputs (lengths, pointers, indexes) are attacker-controlled until checked
Because WebAssembly cannot return integers
To log them
blocks.explain: The RLBox documentation: values from the sandboxed library must be validated before use, because a compromised library could otherwise abuse Firefox code. Tainted types force the host to check, for example, that a length is in range. It is the in-process version of the IPC rule from lesson 5.

lessons.title: Case: CVE-2023-4863, one image library inside everything

blocks.md:
Plain idea: the code that decodes an image format is usually one open-source library, and every browser, chat app and operating system that shows that format carries its own copy. A single bug in it is therefore a bug in thousands of products, each of which has to ship its own fix.

**WebP** is Google's [image format for the web](https://developers.google.com/speed/webp), with lossy and lossless modes; **libwebp** is its reference library. Lossless WebP compresses pixels with **Huffman coding**: frequent symbols get short bit strings, rare ones long strings, and no code is a prefix of another (a *prefix code*), so a decoder can read bits until it recognises a symbol. For speed, decoders expand the code into a **lookup table** indexed by the next few input bits.

The arithmetic that matters: in a table indexed by $n$ bits, a symbol whose code has length $L \le n$ fills $2^{n-L}$ slots. A **complete** prefix code fills the table exactly: $\sum_s 2^{-L_s} = 1$ (the Kraft equality). If the lengths are *over-subscribed* ($\sum_s 2^{-L_s} > 1$), they are not a valid code at all, and filling the table writes more than $2^n$ slots.

libwebp sized its Huffman tables in advance: the [source comment](https://chromium.googlesource.com/webm/libwebp/+/refs/heads/main/src/dec/vp8l_dec.c) explains that the fixed sizes were computed as the worst case for valid codes with the `enough` tool by Mark Adler (co-author of the zlib compression library). The overflow class follows directly: if invalid input can reach the table-building step before it is rejected, it can write past a buffer sized only for valid input. The [fix](https://chromium.googlesource.com/webm/libwebp/+/902bc9190331343b2017211debcec8d2ab87e17a) by Vincent Rabaud (7 September 2023), "Fix OOB write in BuildHuffmanTable", builds in two steps: first check that the code data is valid, and only if it is (and the table is too small) allocate more memory and build.
