blocks.title: Filling an 8-slot table with valid and over-subscribed lengths

scenes.caption: The table has 8 slots (3 index bits) and the heap allocation right after it belongs to something else.
Valid lengths 1, 2, 3, 3: symbol 0 fills 4 slots, symbol 1 two, symbols 2 and 3 one each. Exactly 8: the Kraft sum is 1.
Over-subscribed lengths 1, 1, 2, 2 need 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 12 slots. The vulnerable builder fills slots 0 to 7 with the first two symbols...
...then keeps writing: symbols 2 and 3 land in the neighbouring allocation. Validity is only checked after the loop, too late.
The fixed builder counts first (12 is not 8), rejects the input, and never writes. Valid input still decodes exactly as before.

blocks.md: **What happened.** Apple's Security Engineering and Architecture team (SEAR) and Citizen Lab reported the bug to Chrome on 6 September 2023. On 7 September Citizen Lab [published BLASTPASS](https://citizenlab.ca/2023/09/blastpass-nso-group-iphone-zero-click-zero-day-exploit-captured-in-the-wild/): a zero-click chain (no tap needed) delivering NSO Group's Pegasus spyware to an up-to-date iPhone (iOS 16.6) of someone at a Washington DC civil society organisation, through PassKit (Apple Wallet pass) attachments containing malicious images sent over iMessage. Apple's [iOS 16.6.1](https://support.apple.com/en-us/106361) the same day fixed CVE-2023-41064, a buffer overflow in its image framework ImageIO, and Citizen Lab said Lockdown Mode (Apple's optional hardened mode for people at high risk) blocked the attack. Apple's advisory does not mention libwebp; the shared reporters and timing led many to link the two CVEs, but Apple has not confirmed it.

[Chrome 116.0.5845.187](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2023/09/stable-channel-update-for-desktop_11.html) followed on 11 September, rating CVE-2023-4863 Critical with an exploit in the wild. Mozilla fixed Firefox and Thunderbird on 12 September ([MFSA 2023-40](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2023-40/)), noting the bug had also been tracked as CVE-2023-5129.

A bug in a shared parsing library is a supply-chain event. Inventory where the library is linked (browsers, Electron apps, image tools, mobile apps), not just which browser version users run. CISA's catalog entry for this CVE says it "can affect applications that use the WebP Codec".

blocks.question: In the toy and in libwebp's fix, why validate the whole code before building the table instead of adding a bounds check on each write?
options: Bounds checks are not allowed in C
The table size is unknown
It rejects invalid codes before any write, and once a code is known valid the table can be sized for it, so valid streams still decode with the build loop unchanged
Validation makes the image smaller
blocks.explain: A per-write bounds check would also be memory-safe. The libwebp fix runs the builder first to check validity and, if a valid code needs a bigger table, allocates more memory before filling it, so valid (even unbalanced) streams still decode. The key error in the vulnerable code was writing before knowing the input was valid.

blocks.question: A decoder with a 3-bit (8-slot) table receives code lengths 1, 2, 2, 3. How many slots would building the table need, and what does that say about the input?
options: 9: over-subscribed, so the input is invalid and an unchecked builder writes one slot past the table
8: a complete, valid code
7: incomplete but harmless
12: twice the table
blocks.explain: Length 1 fills 4 slots, each length 2 fills 2, length 3 fills 1: 4 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 9. The Kraft sum is 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/8 = 9/8, more than 1, so no valid prefix code has these lengths. A builder that writes before validating overflows by one slot.

lessons.title: The patch gap: from upstream fix to every Chromium in every app

blocks.md:
Plain idea: a security fix is also a map to the bug. Once a fix is public, anyone can read it, work out what it repairs and attack users who have not installed it yet. The time between a fix becoming visible and reaching users is the window for **n-day** exploitation, and it is longest for the products furthest downstream.

Tiny example: Chromium is open source, so a fix lands in a public repository. Chrome Stable users get it at the next Stable update. An Electron app gets it when Electron ships a release *and* the app's vendor ships an update built on it *and* each user installs that.

Amy Ressler of the Chrome Security Team explained the Chrome side in [August 2023](https://security.googleblog.com/2023/08/an-update-on-chrome-security-updates.html). Chromium fixes land in the public source repository and are discoverable; the time between a patch landing and shipping in a Stable update is the **patch gap**. Chrome ships a new milestone every four weeks with Stable updates in between. Before Chrome 77 the patch gap averaged 35 days; moving to two-weekly Stable updates in 2020 cut it to around 15 days; from Chrome 116 Stable updates became weekly, shipping fixes 3.5 days sooner on average. Chrome treats all Critical and High bugs as if they will be exploited.

Chrome Releases posts also note that access to bug details "may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated", and kept restricted if the bug is in a third-party library other projects depend on but have not yet fixed. The fix itself, though, is public from the moment it lands.

blocks.title: CVE-2023-4863 from report to downstream releases (day 0 = 6 Sep 2023)

scenes.caption: Day 0: Apple SEAR and Citizen Lab report the bug to Chrome. Day 1: the libwebp fix is committed and Apple ships iOS 16.6.1 for its own ImageIO bug, CVE-2023-41064.
Day 5: Chrome 116.0.5845.187. Day 6: Firefox 117.0.1 and Electron 26.2.1, which moved to the fixed Chromium build.
Day 7: libwebp tags 1.3.2, Electron backports the fix to 22, 24 and 25, and CISA adds the CVE to its catalog with a deadline on day 28.
Then the long tail: each app built on Electron or libwebp ships its own update, on its own schedule, and each user installs it. That window, not Chrome's, is where most n-day exposure lives.

blocks.md: **Electron and embedded WebViews.** **Electron** is a framework for building desktop apps from JavaScript, HTML and CSS: each app embeds its own copy of Chromium plus Node.js (the JavaScript runtime used outside browsers), so it carries its own browser engine and its own patch gap. Electron hardening is covered in **JavaScript and Node.js security**. Its [release timeline](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/electron-timelines) ships a major version every 8 weeks, targets even-numbered Chromium versions, and supports the latest three stable majors; the oldest gets only security fixes. Its release notes show fast work on both cases in this course: Electron 26.2.1 moved to the fixed Chromium on 12 September 2023, and 22.3.24, 24.8.3 and 25.8.1 backported the CVE-2023-4863 fix on 13 September; 35.1.2, 34.4.1 and 33.4.8 backported the CVE-2025-2783 fix on 27 March 2025. An app pinned to an unsupported Electron major gets neither.

On Android, the system WebView has been an [updatable component since Lollipop](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/android_webview/docs/webview-providers.md), delivered as a separate package, so its fixes do not wait for a full OS update; recall from lesson 3 that it has no site isolation.

blocks.question: Why does an open-source browser have an n-day problem that a closed-source one has less of?
options: Open-source browsers have more bugs
Security fixes land in a public repository before most users have the update, so the fix itself points attackers at the bug
Open-source code cannot be signed
Closed-source browsers never patch
blocks.explain: Chrome's team says exactly this: fixes are publicly discoverable once landed, and attackers can develop exploits for users who have not updated yet. Closed-source fixes can still be found by diffing patched binaries, but only once the update ships. Shorter release cycles shrink the window.

blocks.question: Chrome's average patch gap went from about 35 days to about 15. What changed?

Site isolation was enabled

blocks.explain: The Chrome security blog attributes the drop to biweekly Stable updates from Chrome 77, with weekly updates from Chrome 116 cutting a further 3.5 days on average.

lessons.title: Defending a fleet: policies, extensions and detection

blocks.md:
Plain idea: as a defender you cannot fix browser bugs, but you control four things: how fast fixes reach every browser and embedded copy, which hardening settings are forced on, which extensions get in, and what you watch for when a sandbox fails.

Tiny example: on one laptop, Chrome auto-updated yesterday, but a coupon extension with access to every site was installed last week, site isolation was switched off by a stale policy, and a chat app runs a two-year-old Electron. Each is a separate gap, and each is visible from management data you can collect.

**Policies that matter for this course** (Chrome's policies are documented in Chromium's [policy definitions](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/components/policy/resources/templates/policy_definitions/Extensions/ExtensionInstallBlocklist.yaml)):

- **Site isolation**: `SitePerProcess` (all sites) or `IsolateOrigins` (a list). When a policy enables it, users cannot disable it. On Android the equivalents end in `Android`.
- **JIT**: `DefaultJavaScriptJitSetting` with per-site allow and block lists (lesson 9).
- **Extensions**: `ExtensionInstallBlocklist` set to `*` blocks all extensions by default; `ExtensionInstallAllowlist` then admits reviewed ones, and blocked extensions already installed are disabled.

**Extensions in the process model.** Chrome's guidance on [staying secure](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/develop/security-privacy/stay-secure) says content scripts (extension code injected into pages) are the most exposed part of an extension: they share the page's renderer process, so a compromised renderer or a side channel reaches them, and messages from a content script "might have been crafted by an attacker". Sensitive work belongs in the extension's service worker, which must validate every message and its sender. Since Chrome 92, desktop site isolation also isolates extensions from each other. The Cyberhaven compromise (December 2024, taught in **XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks**) shows the other risk: a phished publisher account pushed a malicious update of a trusted extension. Manifest V3 (the current version of Chrome's extension platform) requires all extension logic to ship in the package, with no [remotely hosted code](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/develop/migrate/improve-security) or `eval`.

scenes.caption: The fleet is every browser and every embedded Chromium: managed Chrome, Firefox, Electron apps, WebViews.
Prevent: an update pipeline that forces relaunch after security updates, and policies that keep site isolation on and limit JIT where speed is not needed.
Prevent: deny extensions by default and allow reviewed ones. An extension with broad host permissions is a trusted script on every site.
Detect: EDR process trees (a renderer or GPU process starting programs or loading odd DLLs) and crash telemetry (renderer kills and crash spikes on one site).
Respond: track vendor advisories and the CISA KEV catalog, map each CVE to every product that embeds the component, and push updates within the deadline.

blocks.md: **Detection signals that come from the internals in this course:**

- **Process ancestry.** Renderers, GPU and network processes do not start programs (lesson 2). A child process under any of them, or an unsigned DLL loaded into them, is high-signal. Remember Chrome's helpers are identified by `--type=` on the command line.
- **Version drift.** Inventory Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers, Firefox, and every Electron app with its *Electron* version (lesson 12). Compare against the first fixed version in each vendor advisory.
- **Crash patterns.** Hardening turns many failed exploitation attempts into renderer crashes (aborting bounds checks, bad-message kills, sandbox violations). Crash spikes tied to one site or one link in email deserve triage.
- **Delivery.** The two campaigns in this course with public delivery details used emailed links: one-time links (CVE-2021-30551) and personalised, short-lived invitations (CVE-2025-2783); BLASTPASS instead used iMessage attachments. Mail and proxy logs of who clicked what, and when, make it possible to scope an incident after an advisory lands.

**Response** follows the advisory: update every affected product, force a relaunch (an update does not protect a browser that keeps running the old binary), and for confirmed compromise treat the host as an endpoint incident, since a sandbox escape means code ran with the user's privileges.

The defender's three questions for every browser CVE: which of our products embed this component, which versions contain the fix, and how many hosts are still running an older build right now (not just installed it)?

blocks.question: Your EDR shows a Chromium helper process with `--type=gpu-process` loading a DLL from a user's temp folder. What is the best first reading?
options: Normal GPU driver behaviour
An extension update
Possible sandbox escape or injection into a privileged child; collect the DLL, the parent tree and the browser version, and check recent advisories
A Site Isolation process swap
blocks.explain: The GPU process is a known escape target and loads drivers from system locations, not from a temp folder. Treat it as possible compromise: preserve evidence, identify the browser build, and check whether a known in-the-wild CVE fits.

blocks.question: An extension's service worker performs privileged actions when a content script sends `{action: 'export', site: ...}`. What should it do with that message?
options: Treat it as possibly attacker-crafted: validate the sender and the request against what that tab is allowed to do
Trust it, because content scripts run in an isolated world
Forward it to the page
Evaluate it with eval
blocks.explain: Chrome's guidance: content scripts are the most exposed part of an extension and their messages may be crafted by an attacker. It is the same rule as Mojo in lesson 5, one layer up.

lessons.title: Who finds browser bugs: bounties, in-the-wild 0-days and practice

blocks.md:
Plain idea: browser bugs are found by three groups with different incentives. Vendor teams and their fuzzers find many internally (Chrome Releases posts credit "internal audits, fuzzing and other initiatives"); outside researchers report them for bug bounties; and attackers (often commercial spyware vendors) find or buy them to use as 0-days. Defenders mostly learn about the third group from advisories saying "an exploit exists in the wild".

Tiny example: Chrome's 2024 bounty programme received 337 valid security bug reports and paid 137 outside researchers. Separately, Chrome Releases posts mark individual fixes with "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-... exists in the wild". Those are the ones attackers found first, and each went through the same process you have seen: report, fix, Stable update, and a race against the patch gap.

**Bounty economics.** Google's [2024 review](https://blog.google/security/vulnerability-reward-program-2024-in/) of its Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) reports, for Chrome: 337 reports of unique, valid security bugs; 137 researchers rewarded; USD 3.4 million paid. The top Chrome award, USD 100,115, was for a MiraclePtr bypass. Chrome restructured rewards that year to push research toward the deepest targets: up to USD 250,000 for demonstrating code execution in the browser or another non-sandboxed process, the MiraclePtr Bypass Reward raised to USD 250,128, and the first V8 Sandbox Bypass rewards. The rules live in the [Chrome VRP rules](https://bughunters.google.com/about/rules/chrome-friends/5745167867576320/chrome-vulnerability-reward-program-rules).

Read the structure as a defender: the highest rewards go to breaking the containment layers (sandbox, MiraclePtr, V8 sandbox), because those layers are what turn a renderer bug into "only" High.

blocks.md:
**Two more in-the-wild cases, at advisory level.**

- **CVE-2019-5786** (March 2019): a use-after-free in [FileReader](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/FileReader), the web API that lets a page read the contents of files and blobs, reported by Clement Lecigne of TAG on 27 February and fixed in [Chrome 72.0.3626.121](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2019/03/stable-channel-update-for-desktop.html) on 1 March. Google's [disclosure post](https://security.googleblog.com/2019/03/disclosing-vulnerabilities-to-protect.html) says it was exploited together with a Windows bug: a NULL pointer dereference in the `win32k.sys` kernel driver, a privilege escalation usable as a sandbox escape, which Google believed exploitable only on Windows 7 because of mitigations in newer Windows.

- **CVE-2024-4671** (May 2024): a use-after-free in Chrome's Visuals component, reported anonymously on 7 May and fixed two days later in [Chrome 124.0.6367.201/.202](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/2024/05/stable-channel-update-for-desktop_9.html), with Google aware of an in-the-wild exploit. Few details are public; CISA's catalog describes heap corruption via a crafted HTML page affecting multiple Chromium-based browsers.

TAG counted [33 in-the-wild 0-days disclosed in the first half of 2021](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/how-we-protect-users-0-day-attacks/), 11 more than in all of 2020.

blocks.md: **Where to practise, legally.** Only test software you own or have written permission to test; anything else can be a crime under laws such as the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and the UK Computer Misuse Act.

- **Your own browser**: open `chrome://process-internals` to see the Site Isolation mode and how frames map to processes, and match your OS process list to the `--type=` switches from lesson 2.
- **Read advisories weekly**: follow [Chrome Releases](https://chromereleases.googleblog.com/) and [Mozilla security advisories](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/), and run this course's version checker against your own machines and Electron apps.
- **Memory bugs hands-on**: [pwn.college](https://pwn.college/) and [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) teach memory-corruption bugs and mitigations in provided labs.
- **Reading code**: Chromium's [Rule of 2](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/rule-of-2.md) and [Mojo security guidance](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/mojo.md) are short; review an open-source IPC handler against them as an exercise.
- **Reporting**: if you do find a browser bug, report it through the vendor's programme (the Chrome VRP rules above, or Mozilla's bug bounty) rather than publishing it.

Across every case in this course the pattern is the same: one bug class (type confusion, use-after-free, a stale check, a trusted value from a less privileged process), one boundary it crossed, and one fix that either corrects the logic or moves the boundary. Defenders win the n-day race by knowing which of their products sit behind which boundary.

blocks.question: Why does Chrome pay as much for a MiraclePtr bypass as for code execution outside the sandbox?
options: MiraclePtr bugs are easier to find
A bypass would make a whole class of contained bugs exploitable again, so Chrome prices it like the outcome the layer prevents
MiraclePtr runs in the kernel
It is a typo in the reward table
blocks.explain: MiraclePtr turns many browser-process use-after-frees into unexploitable bugs. A bypass would undo that for a whole class, which is why Google says it restructured rewards in 2024 to encourage this deeper research.

blocks.question: CISA added CVE-2023-4863, CVE-2024-4671 and CVE-2025-2783 to its KEV catalog. How long did US federal agencies get to remediate each, per the catalog data?
options: 7 days
14 days
60 days
21 days
blocks.explain: The script's output shows dateAdded and dueDate 21 days apart for all three. Chromium's own target for in-the-wild bugs is 7 days or less; its 60-day target is for High bugs without exploitation evidence.
